items.title: JSON Schema 2020-12 and the Contract for Context | ​Ola Hungerford | MCP Release Party - Seattle
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
Session 2: Say What You Mean: JSON Schema 2020-12 and the Contract for Context

​In MCP, the schema is the contract for context. It's how a tool tells a model what goes in and what comes out. MCP originally shipped a three-keyword subset of JSON Schema, a reasonable bet on the lowest common denominator across a fragmented landscape of LLM APIs. Two SEPs later, tool schemas conform to JSON Schema 2020-12, the same default dialect as OpenAPI 3.1. This talk will cover examples of what that unlocks, what it doesn't fix, and what client and server authors need to change in the new specification.

​About Speaker:
​Ola Hungerford is a Principal Engineer at Nordstrom and a maintainer and community moderator for the Model Context Protocol. She leads AI enablement initiatives while contributing to MCP's specification, developer tooling, documentation, and community governance. Ola comes from a diverse technical background spanning two decades, including personalisation systems and enterprise platforms. She's also a vocalist and songwriter who experiments with augmenting human creativity through technology.

About the Event:
This session was presented at the MCP Release Party hosted on July 28th at Microsoft Reactor in Seattle area. ​This event was hosted as a part of a series of MCP Release Parties taking place simultaneously in cities around the world.

items.title: MCP Goes Stateless | ​John Dellenbaugh & Pankaj Kumar | MCP Release Party - Seattle
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
​Session 1: MCP Goes Stateless

​The new MCP specification (2026-07-28) makes the protocol stateless. We will break down what this change is, why it matters, and then dig into it together with a live demo.

​About Speakers:
​John Dellenbaugh is a Software Engineering Manager, most recently at Microsoft, where he spent 19 years delivering cloud, security, and AI work with a hands-on background in software security, network security, and Zero Trust identity. He now works as a founding engineer at an early-stage AI startup on MCP architecture, vector search, and agent workflows.

​Pankaj Kumar is a Software Developer at Amazon with a deep interest in MLOps, especially the infrastructure and emerging standards for running AI agents in production. Outside of work, he is a big fan of Lord of the Rings, anime, and manga.

About the Event:
This session was presented at the MCP Release Party hosted on July 28th at Microsoft Reactor in Seattle area. ​This event was hosted as a part of a series of MCP Release Parties taking place simultaneously in cities around the world.

items.title: Events Notifications in MCP | ​Aman Singh | MCP Release Party - Seattle
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
​Session 4: Events Notifications in MCP

​MCP, the protocol agents use to reach tools and data, can notify a client only while it holds a connection open, and mostly only that something changed, not what. That's about to change. An MCP working group is drafting Events, an upcoming protocol extension that lets agents subscribe to structured event streams. This talk is a brief tour of the proposal and how it is going to shape real-time events in MCP.

​About Speaker:
​Aman Singh is a Principal Software Engineer in the Office of Azure's CTO, where he focuses on Agentic Software Engineering and is a maintainer of Drasi, a CNCF Sandbox project for change-driven architectures. He has had more than 12 years of distributed systems experience at LinkedIn and Microsoft, spanning stream processing (Kafka, Samza), cloud migration, and building new Azure services from the ground up.

About the Event:
This session was presented at the MCP Release Party hosted on July 28th at Microsoft Reactor in Seattle area. ​This event was hosted as a part of a series of MCP Release Parties taking place simultaneously in cities around the world.

items.title: Reading Group July 2026 - Loop Engineering
items.author: AAIF Live
items.summary:
// Abstract
Loop engineering is the shift from manually prompting AI agents turn-by-turn to designing autonomous systems that do the prompting for you. Instead of writing a prompt, reading output, then writing the next prompt, you build a small control system that discovers work, delegates tasks to agents (and sub-agents), verifies results, persists state, and decides what to do next on a schedule or until a goal is met. It sits one level above agent harness engineering: where a harness equips a single agent run, a loop keeps firing agents on a cadence, spawning helpers, and feeding itself. The framing is increasingly tool-agnostic, as both Claude Code and OpenAI Codex have converged on similar primitives. The people building at the frontier are already living it: Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code at Anthropic, has said his job is no longer writing prompts but writing the loops that do.
